bill.title: Providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to "California State Motor Vehicle Pollution Control Standards; Notice of Decision Granting a Waiver of Clean Air Act Preemption for California's Advanced Clean Car Program and a Within the Scope Confirmation for California's Zero Emission Vehicle Amendments for 2017 and Earlier Model Years".
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

classification.plainSummary: This resolution would block an Environmental Protection Agency rule that granted California a waiver to enforce its own vehicle emissions standards, including its Advanced Clean Car Program and Zero Emission Vehicle requirements for 2017 and earlier model years. If passed, the resolution would disapprove the waiver and prevent California from applying stricter pollution control standards than federal law for those vehicles. The measure uses the Congressional Review Act, which allows Congress to overturn recently issued federal regulations.

industries.rationale: Automotive manufacturers are directly affected by whether California can enforce separate vehicle emissions and zero-emission vehicle standards.
Zero-emission vehicle mandates reduce gasoline demand, affecting petroleum refining and distribution markets.
Electric vehicle adoption drives demand for charging infrastructure and electricity from renewable sources.
Increased electric vehicle use affects electricity demand and grid infrastructure planning.

method.formula: score = Σ_industries ( donorShare(industry) × billWeight(industry) ), where billWeight = classifierConfidence / Σ classifierConfidence. Range 0–1, read as a weighted share of disclosed itemized money.

ordinary.text: They wrote this bill. Sponsoring a bill about your own district's industry is the ordinary case, not the odd one.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
